seoTitle: How to Add a Calendar to Notion (Page, Dashboard, Database)
metaDescription: Add a calendar to Notion by creating a database and switching its layout to Calendar, then embed it on any page or dashboard. Free on every plan.
intro: Notion doesn't have a separate "insert calendar" button. A calendar in Notion is a database wearing a Calendar layout, and any database needs at least one date property before that layout does anything useful. That's what makes it flexible enough to sit on its own page, live inside a dashboard, or track the same tasks you already manage in a table. This guide covers the fastest way to start one, how to point it at the right date field, and how to put the same calendar in more than one place without duplicating your data.

steps.heading: Start a calendar database
steps.body: The quickest route is a new page: open the sidebar, add a blank page, and under "Get started with" click the ••• menu and choose Calendar. Notion builds a database with a date property already in place and switches straight to the Calendar layout. If you'd rather build it manually, or add one inline on a page you already have, type /Calendar view and press enter, or add a database block and pick New empty database from the panel that opens, then switch its layout in the next step. Either path lands in the same place; the template shortcut just skips a step.

image.caption: A blank new page in the Notion sidebar, ready to hold the calendar — sitting alongside existing pages like Content Calendar and Goals Tracker.

steps.heading: Building it manually: create the database first
steps.body: If you went the database-block route, Notion opens a New database panel with a few starting options: New empty database, Build with AI, Import CSV, or linking to a database you already have, plus a shortlist of suggested databases like Creative Projects or Tasks Tracker. For a calendar meant to hold its own events, New empty database is the simplest path. For a calendar meant to visualize an existing project's due dates, skip ahead and add a Calendar view to that database instead of creating a new one.

image.caption: The New database panel, offering an empty database, AI-built database, CSV import, or a link to an existing database like Content Calendar.

steps.heading: Switch the layout to Calendar
steps.body: A database you built manually defaults to a table layout, so open the layout menu and choose Calendar from the grid of options alongside Table, Board, Timeline, List, Gallery, Chart, and Feed. Selecting it changes how the same underlying data displays: instead of rows, you get a month grid with items placed on the date pulled from a date property. A database needs at least one property of that type for Calendar to have anything to show.

image.caption: The Layout panel with Calendar selected. The same database can switch between Table, Board, Timeline, and other views without losing any data.

steps.heading: Point it at the right date field
steps.body: Below the layout grid, two settings control behavior. "Show calendar by" picks which date property drives placement, which matters if your database has more than one, like a start date and a separate due date. "Show calendar as" switches between Month and Week. If items aren't showing up where expected, check this setting first: the calendar only reflects whichever date property it's set to read from, not every date field on the page.

steps.heading: Put the calendar somewhere else
steps.body: To surface it outside its own page, open a dashboard page, type /, and search for the calendar's page name to insert it as a linked view, or copy the database block and paste it in. Either way keeps it synced to the same underlying data, so an event added from the dashboard shows up identically on the calendar's own page. If you'd rather see deadlines from a database you already use, like a Content Calendar or Goals Tracker, add a new Calendar view directly on that database instead of building a separate one. That keeps a single source of truth: tasks stay in one place, and the calendar becomes another way to look at the same records instead of a duplicate list you update by hand.

troubleshooting.problem: An item doesn't appear anywhere on the calendar
troubleshooting.cause: It has no value set in the date property the calendar is reading from, or "Show calendar by" is pointed at a different date property than the one that's filled in.
troubleshooting.fix: Open the item and confirm the relevant date field has a value, then check the calendar's "Show calendar by" setting matches that property.

troubleshooting.problem: You end up with two separate lists of the same tasks
troubleshooting.cause: A new, unrelated database was created for the calendar instead of adding a Calendar view to the existing project database.
troubleshooting.fix: Delete the duplicate database and add a Calendar view directly on the original one instead.

faq.question: Is the Notion calendar feature free?
faq.answer: Yes. Calendar is one of the built-in database layouts available on Notion's free plan, alongside Table, Board, Timeline, List, and Gallery.

faq.question: Can I turn an existing database into a calendar view?
faq.answer: Yes. Open the database, add a new view, and choose Calendar as the layout. Any item with a value in a date property places itself on the calendar automatically.

faq.question: Does the calendar update automatically when I add new tasks?
faq.answer: Yes, because Calendar is just a view of the underlying database. Add or edit an item from any view and every other view of that same database reflects the change instantly.

faq.question: Can I have multiple calendars on one dashboard?
faq.answer: Yes. You can embed calendar views from different databases on the same dashboard page, so a content calendar and a personal goals calendar sit side by side.

faq.question: What's the difference between the Calendar layout and Notion Calendar?
faq.answer: The Calendar layout described here is a database view inside your workspace. Notion Calendar is a separate scheduling app that syncs with Google Calendar accounts. Related, but a different product from embedding a calendar view on a page.
